title: Cold & Flu Relief

drivers.name: Price increase (6.2%)
drivers.evidence: Past promotions show noise-adjusted lift of x1.4 at deeper discounts; this is a price increase, not a promotion. The prior week at $12.03 saw 24 units (x1.27 vs baseline), suggesting limited demand drop, but no promotion means price sensitivity likely reduces demand. Apply moderate downside.

drivers.name: Store closed Monday
drivers.evidence: One day lost in a 7-day week. No past closure data for this product, but store closures reduce sales. Adjust for lost selling day. Noise-adjusted effect shrunk due to lack of evidence.

adjustment.analysis: The target week has no events, but a price increase to $12.03 (+6.2%) and a store closure on Monday. The price rise is above recent levels (previous $11.33), and past promotions at similar or deeper discounts show a noise-adjusted lift of x1.4. However, this price increase is not a promotion, so it likely reduces demand. The prior week (2026-10-05) saw 24 units at $12.03, above baseline (18.9), but this may reflect carryover or unexplained noise. The store closure on Monday reduces selling days, likely lowering sales. No past evidence shows a closure effect, but one day lost in a 7-day week implies ~14% sales loss. The baseline trend is down (-11.8% over 13 weeks), but the target week is not seasonal. The uplift model suggests no change, but judgment overrides this: price increase and closure both reduce demand. Shrink effect due to limited evidence.

brief:
PRODUCT: Cold & Flu Relief | category Health | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 12.03 (+6.2% vs regular price 11.33)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 18.9 | 5%-95%: 6.2 - 35.5 | 10%-90%: 9.5 - 31.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-46% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
